newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. Gov. says Assembly would 'undo' workfare.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. Gov. says Assembly would 'undo' workfare.

text.p: Gov. George Pataki on Wednesday castigated the Assembly's new welfare plan, saying it would "undo" workfare programs that oblige those who get benefits to work, and fail to meet the new federal law.

Saying the only aspect of the Assembly Democrats' plan that he liked was its adopting the five-year time limit for cash benefits for families required under the new federal law, Pataki faulted his opponents for wanting to continue cash benefits for single, able-bodied adults for two years.

And the Republican governor accused the Assembly of drafting a bill that would force counties to hire workfare participants after six months and burden localities with expensive mandates, causing them to raise property taxes.

"That would be very costful to the local governments. It would immediately make us a magnet for people who want government jobs because it would place them in workfare and make them automatically eligible for a government job at the end of six months, and it would just clearly undo our ability to have any form of workfare," he told reporters in Albany.
A spokeswoman for Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, was not immediately available to comment.

New York State faces big challenges in adapting its laws to the federal program enacted last August, even though it was projected to get a huge windfall during the first year, as the state constitution obliges it to care for the needy.

Pataki said the Assembly's plan to require workfare participants to be paid the prevailing wage would make it too costly for the state to comply with Washington's mandate that they work 20 hours a week.
"It would bankrupt the system," he said, explaining beneficiaries who worked a 20-hour week at the prevailing wage, which is higher than the minimum wage, would be doing better than other workers.

Saluting the workfare programs of New York City and Westchester County for working with unions to ensure that participants supplemented the government's workforce instead of replacing it, Pataki said the Assembly's plan would derail those types of efforts.
"This would undo them completely. This would make it utterly impossible," he said.
